content: In the year 2000, fire-related burns and smoke inhalation were responsible for approximately 238,000 deaths worldwide, equating to a mortality rate of 3.9 deaths per 100,000 individuals. The majority of these fatalities occurred among children and individuals under the age of 44. The presence of smoke alarms in residential settings has been associated with a decreased risk of death due to residential fires. This study aimed to evaluate various interventions designed to promote the ownership and functionality of residential smoke alarms. The goal was to assess their impact on the prevalence of owned and operational smoke alarms, as well as their influence on the incidence of fires, burns, and other fire-related injuries. To identify relevant trials, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group's specialized register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Dissertation Abstracts, IBSS, ISTP, FIREDOC, and LRC. Additional sources such as conference proceedings, published case studies, bibliographies, and direct contact with investigators and organizations were also utilized. Most searches were last updated in September 2007. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or non-randomized controlled trials conducted or published after 1969 that evaluated interventions aimed at promoting residential smoke alarms. Data extraction and trial quality assessment were independently performed by two authors. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials was conducted to calculate odds ratios (OR) between intervention and control groups using a random-effects model. A chi-square test for heterogeneity was applied with a significance threshold of 10%. Results from non-randomized trials were described narratively. A total of 26 trials were identified, of which 17 were randomized controlled trials. Overall, interventions involving counseling and education, with or without the provision of free or discounted smoke alarms, resulted in a modest increase in the likelihood of owning a smoke alarm (OR = 1.21; 95% CI 0.89 to 1.64) and having an installed, functional smoke alarm (OR = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.80). The addition of free or discounted smoke alarms to educational interventions did not significantly alter these outcomes. However, the results were sensitive to the quality of the trials. Counseling provided as part of primary care child health surveillance demonstrated a somewhat greater effect on smoke alarm ownership (OR = 1.96; 95% CI 1.03 to 3.72) and functionality (OR = 1.46; 95% CI 1.15 to 1.85). These findings were generally supported by non-randomized trials evaluating similar interventions. Only one randomized controlled trial reported injury outcomes. This trial found no significant effect of a smoke alarm give-away program on the total number of injuries (rate ratio 1.3; 95% CI 0.9 to 1.9) or on hospitalizations and deaths (rate ratio 1.3; 95% CI 0.7 to 2.3). In contrast, a non-randomized trial evaluating a similar give-away program reported a substantial reduction in serious injuries. Neither trial demonstrated a beneficial effect on the occurrence of fires. Mass media and community education interventions showed minimal benefit in multiple non-randomized trials. Two trials, one of which was randomized, indicated that smoke alarm installation programs increased the likelihood of having a functional smoke alarm. Additionally, the non-randomized trial reported reductions in fire-related injuries. In conclusion, this review found that programs aimed at promoting smoke alarms generally have modest effects on increasing smoke alarm ownership and functionality. There is no clear evidence that these programs reduce the incidence of fires or fire-related injuries. Counseling as part of child health surveillance appears to have a slightly greater impact on smoke alarm ownership and functionality, but its effects on injury outcomes remain unassessed. Community-based smoke alarm give-away programs have not been shown to significantly increase smoke alarm prevalence or reduce fire-related injuries. Similarly, community education programs have not demonstrated a reduction in burns or fire-related injuries. Smoke alarm installation programs may increase the prevalence of functional alarms and potentially reduce fire-related injuries, but these findings require further confirmation. Additionally, the cost-effectiveness of such programs has not been evaluated. Future efforts to promote smoke alarms through installation programs should be assessed using well-designed randomized controlled trials that measure both injury outcomes and cost-effectiveness.
